diagnostics.message: Semicolon present; review for clause stacking.
diagnostics.text: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, ahead of total retail demand at 1.8%; both accelerated materially. Retail electricity prices are up 5.1%, also a material acceleration. Net planned generation additions now total 227.6 GW, but this is a pipeline measure rather than operating supply. The combination points to a more demanding power environment without showing that AI is the sole or primary cause of demand or price growth.

diagnostics.message: Semicolon present; review for clause stacking.
diagnostics.text: The buildout is also meeting a more demanding power environment. Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, compared with 1.8% for total retail demand, and retail prices are up 5.1%; each accelerated materially. Supply pipelines appear large on separate measures: net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW, while active interconnection queues contain 2,061 GW. Yet only 24.2% of the queue has reached an executed agreement or construction, and historically 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. These figures do not attribute rising demand or prices to AI, but they show why planned capacity should not be treated as power already available to new computing loads.

diagnostics.message: Semicolon present; review for clause stacking.
diagnostics.text: The labor signals remain considerably narrower. Only one tracked AI-linked channel is adding jobs; power and communication construction leads at 0.8%, while two channels have positive real-earnings growth. Reuters also reported job cuts as companies shift investment toward AI, including a planned 5,000-role reduction at Barclays. Economy-wide productivity and real output are growing 2.2% and 2.5%, respectively, but real hourly compensation growth is 0.6%. Those aggregate outcomes cannot isolate AI’s contribution, and they have not coincided with broad employment growth across the tracked channels.
